Keep rows that match a condition

Source: R/filter.R
filter.tbl_gpu.Rd

filter() keeps the rows of a GPU table where every condition is TRUE, as dplyr::filter() does. The conditions listed under "Supported expressions" run on the GPU, within the limits stated there, with dplyr's rules for which rows are kept and for NA (see "NA semantics" below). Other conditions run in dplyr on the CPU.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'tbl_gpu'
filter(.data, ..., .by = NULL, .preserve = FALSE)

Arguments

.data

A tbl_gpu object created by tbl_gpu().

...

Logical expressions to filter by (see "Supported expressions" below). Multiple expressions, whether passed as separate dots or combined with & within one dot, are combined with AND (a row is kept only if every expression is TRUE for it).

.by

Optional grouping columns for this call only (tidyselect), run on the GPU: filter(df, x > mean(x), .by = g) gives the same rows as df |> group_by(g) |> filter(x > mean(x)) |> ungroup(), and the result is ungrouped. Supplying .by when .data is already grouped (via group_by()) is an error, as in dplyr.

.preserve

Whether to keep the groups the filter emptied. With TRUE, a group_by()-grouped result keeps the input's group keys (empty groups included) for group_data(), collect() and summarise(), like dplyr (see group_by.tbl_gpu() for what carries them on). FALSE recomputes the groups from the remaining rows.

Value

A tbl_gpu object containing only rows where all conditions are TRUE. The GPU memory for the filtered result is newly allocated.

Details

Supported expressions

All the conditions of one filter() call are combined into a single predicate and evaluated together on the GPU, however many dots there are and however deeply they nest. These run on the GPU:

  • Comparisons: ==, !=, <, <=, >, >= – against a literal, another column, an R variable, or an arithmetic expression ((x - y) > 0); for strings, see the string item below

  • Logic: &, |, !, xor(), nested to any depth (x > 2 & (y < 5 | z == 1)); &&/|| are an error that points at &/|

  • is.na()

  • %in%, including a set containing NA (as in R, %in% is never NA: an NA value is TRUE when the set contains NA and FALSE otherwise) and an empty set (character(0), c(), etc.: FALSE for every row, NA rows included)

  • between(x, lo, hi) (dplyr's definition: x >= lo & x <= hi, with its NA propagation), near(x, y, tol = ) (abs(x - y) < tol, as dplyr::near())

  • String comparisons, against a literal or another string column. ==, !=, %in% and between() always run on the GPU. <, <=, > and >= compare strings in byte order on the GPU, while R uses the session's collation, so they run on the GPU only when Sys.getlocale("LC_COLLATE") is "C" or "POSIX"; under any other collation ("en_US.UTF-8", say) the call runs in dplyr on the CPU. The same holds for min() and max() of a string column.

  • Column-vs-column comparisons for every operator above

  • Math on columns inside a predicate (+ - * / %% %/% ^, sqrt, log, abs, etc. – the same set mutate() supports)

  • if_else(), case_when(), coalesce(), na_if(), case_match(), recode() (scalar literal shapes), recode_values(), replace_values(), replace_when() – the same conditional/vector functions mutate() supports (see its own docs for the exact type-unification rules), usable anywhere inside a predicate, including as the whole predicate itself (e.g. filter(case_when(x > 1 ~ TRUE, .default = FALSE)))

  • when_any(...)/when_all(...) – particularly useful inside filter() to combine several comma-separated conditions with | instead of & (e.g. filter(when_any(x > 10, y < 0)))

  • The .data/.env pronouns, and ordinary R symbols (a bare name that matches a column resolves to that column; otherwise it is looked up as an R variable: columns shadow the environment, as in dplyr)

  • Window and aggregate functions, anywhere inside a predicate, also next to plain column comparisons in the same dot (filter(x > mean(x) & y < 5)): row_number()/row_number(x), min_rank()/dense_rank()/ percent_rank()/cume_dist(), lag()/lead(), cumsum()/cummax()/cummin()/cumprod()/cummean()/ cumall()/cumany()/consecutive_id(), ntile(), mean()/sum()/min()/max()/n()/sd()/var()/median()/ n_distinct()/first()/last()/nth() – the same set mutate() supports (see its own docs for exact semantics/argument support), evaluated per group when .data is grouped (with group_by() or .by, which behave the same). As in dplyr, a grouped filter keeps the original row order; it does not reorder rows by group.

Comparing a number with a string (filter(mpg > "2")) compares them as strings, as R does; that call runs in dplyr on the CPU.

Multi-dot semantics with window/aggregate predicates

Multiple dots (or multiple &-joined predicates within one dot) are combined with AND, and, as in dplyr, every dot is evaluated against the same input rows, never against the rows an earlier dot left. So filter(x > 0, cumsum(x) < 10) computes cumsum(x) over every row of the input, then combines that with x > 0; it does not keep x > 0 first and compute cumsum() over the remaining rows (which would usually give a smaller cumulative sum and a different result).

NA semantics

filter() keeps a row only if its combined predicate is TRUE (not FALSE and not NA), as in dplyr:

  • filter(x > 5) drops rows where x is NA (the comparison is NA, and NA isn't kept)

  • &/| use R's three-valued logic: NA & FALSE is FALSE, NA | TRUE is TRUE, NA & TRUE/NA | FALSE/NA & NA/ NA | NA are all NA

  • filter(x > 2 | is.na(x)) is the idiom for "keep NA rows too", as in dplyr

  • %in% never gives NA (see "Supported expressions" above), as R's %in% and match()

  • filter(TRUE) returns .data unchanged, with no GPU work; filter(FALSE) and filter(NA) both return zero rows

A floating NaN (e.g. a computed 0/0) stays a value on the GPU, but is.na(), the six comparisons and coalesce() read it as missing, as in R: NaN > 1 is NA (the row is dropped) and is.na(NaN) is TRUE. is.nan() runs on the GPU too.

Conditions that run on the CPU

A condition outside the list above (an R function with no GPU version, for example) is handled in one of two ways. A dot that reads no table column (a pre-computed logical vector, rep(TRUE, n)) is evaluated once in R, with no data mask: a logical scalar is a constant predicate. On an ungrouped filter() a logical vector is a row mask: all the vectors of one call are sized against the input table (a wrong size is dplyr's own error) and combined with & with the call's other predicates, which see the same input rows. On a grouped, .by or rowwise table, or in filter_out(), a logical vector runs the whole call in dplyr. A dot that reads a table column but can't run on the GPU, or that visibly calls something reaching the data mask by name (exists("x"), get("ok")), runs the whole call in dplyr on the CPU (see getOption("cuplyr.fallback") below to be notified when it does). The check reads the dot's syntax, so an alias of such a function or a user function calling it is not seen and has no data mask when the dot names no column. A lazy .data with pending operations runs them early, on the GPU, when a logical vector needs the row count (a plan break, see getOption("cuplyr.plan_break")).

options(cuplyr.fallback = ...)

Controls whether a CPU fallback (the one described above, and every other verb that runs in dplyr on the CPU) notifies the caller. One of:

  • "silent" (default) - no notification

  • "warn" (or "warning") - emits a warning naming the verb, the expression, the reason and the size collected

  • "error" - stop()s instead of falling back

A lazy plan that only runs early on the GPU is a plan break, reported under options(cuplyr.plan_break = ) instead. See cuplyr-fallback.

Performance

Filtering on the GPU is highly parallel. For the best performance, use the conditions listed under "Supported expressions", which run on the GPU, rather than ones that run in dplyr on the CPU.

See also

mutate.tbl_gpu for creating new columns, select.tbl_gpu for selecting columns, collect.tbl_gpu for retrieving results

Examples

library(dplyr)
if (has_gpu()) {
  gpu_mtcars <- tbl_gpu(mtcars)

  # Filter with single condition
  efficient_cars <- gpu_mtcars |>
    filter(mpg > 25)

  # Multiple conditions (combined with AND)
  result <- gpu_mtcars |>
    filter(mpg > 20) |>
    filter(cyl == 4) |>
    collect()

  # Compare two columns
  gpu_cars <- tbl_gpu(cars)
  fast_stops <- gpu_cars |>
    filter(dist < speed) |>
    collect()
}
